DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) -- The worldwide economic recession has exposed a "crisis of global governance" that can only be addressed by the radical reform of the United Nations, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said Wednesday as the World Economic Forum got under way in Switzerland. Kofi Annan says the United Nations needs to be reformed. "The current architecture of managing global affairs is broken and needs to be fixed," Annan said on the opening morning of the five-day annual meeting of global political and business leaders. "We have major new players coming on the scene and they need to be integrated and given a voice." Referring to the U.N. Security Council, which gives permanent places and vetoing powers to the U.S., the UK, Russia, China and France, Annan said: "We cannot continue to run the world based on countries that won a war 60 years ago. It's either destructive competition or cooperation. We live in an interdependent world and the only way to move forward is to cooperate." Annan is one of six co-chairs at this year's WEF gathering, along with news tycoon Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning of the German chemical group Bayer, Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra and Maria Ramos, Chief Executive of the South African transport group Transnet. He also urged delegates to address three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security, and climate change. "It is important leaders work on ways of finding effective, far-reaching policies -- even if they are radical -- that will allow us to create sustainable economic growth and create jobs for those who are out of jobs," Annan said. Newscorp. CEO Murdoch said delegates needed to be "absolutely honest about where the world is at this point," warning that the consequences of $50 trillion being wiped off personal fortunes had left people feeling "depressed and traumatized." "We've been living in the Western world way above our means. We've been on a great binge and it's come to an end and we have to live though the correction," Murdoch said. But he said the downturn offered a chance to set about tackling issues of energy sufficiency and pollution. "We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. This is a time to shape the policies to help to solve some of those problems." HSBC boss Green said the banking industry needed to admit that it had not "covered itself in glory" in contributing to the collapse of the financial industry and called for continuing government intervention to "stop a nasty recession spiraling down into something else." But he said the major banks could contribute to solving the crisis as well: "I do not believe for a moment that you can have a successful economy without successful and properly functioning international capital markets." Wenning said he didn't expect any solutions to emerge from this year's meeting, but hoped delegates could achieve "a joint understanding of the reasons for the financial crisis" and called for a return to "the basics of sustainable behavior." "If we are really able to address these mega-challenges of the future then we would be able to restore the trust in leadership -- and I believe the world needs leadership." Political leaders will join the discussions later Wednesday with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both due to deliver agenda-setting addresses.

Security Council, which grants permanent seats and veto powers to the U.S., the UK, Russia, China, and France, Annan said: “We cannot continue to run the world based on countries that won a war 60 years ago. It’s either destructive competition or cooperation. We live in an interdependent world, and the only way to move forward is to cooperate.”

Annan is one of six co-chairs at this year’s WEF gathering, alongside media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning of the German chemical group Bayer, Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra, and Maria Ramos, Chief Executive of the South African transport group Transnet.

He also urged delegates to confront three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security, and climate change.

“It is important leaders work on ways of finding effective, far-reaching policies—even if they are radical—that will allow us to create sustainable economic growth and create jobs for those who are out of jobs,” Annan said.

News Corp. CEO Murdoch said delegates needed to be “absolutely honest about where the world is at this point,” warning that the consequences of $50 trillion being wiped off personal fortunes had left people feeling “depressed and traumatized.”

“We’ve been living in the Western world way above our means. We’ve been on a great binge, and it’s come to an end, and we have to live through the correction,” Murdoch said.

But he said the downturn offered an opportunity to tackle issues of energy sufficiency and pollution. “We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. This is a time to shape the policies to help solve some of those problems.”

HSBC Chairman Green said the banking industry needed to acknowledge that it had not “covered itself in glory” in contributing to the collapse of the financial industry, and he called for continued government intervention to “stop a nasty recession spiraling down into something else.”

DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) — As the World Economic Forum opened in Switzerland on Wednesday, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said the global recession had revealed a serious failure in the way international affairs are managed, arguing that only sweeping changes to the United Nations could resolve it.

Annan said the U.N. must undergo reform. Speaking on the first morning of the five-day yearly gathering of political and business leaders from around the world, he said the existing system for handling global issues no longer works and must be repaired. He added that important emerging powers are now entering the global stage and should be included in decision-making and allowed to have influence.

Discussing the U.N. Security Council, where the United States, Britain, Russia, China and France hold permanent seats and veto authority, Annan said the world should not still be governed according to the countries that prevailed in a war six decades ago. He warned that nations face a choice between damaging rivalry and collaboration, stressing that because the world is interconnected, cooperation is the only practical path ahead.

Annan is serving as one of six co-chairs of this year’s World Economic Forum. The other co-chairs are media magnate Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Bayer’s Werner Wenning, Indian businessman Anand G. Mahindra and Maria Ramos, chief executive of South African transport company Transnet.

He also called on participants to focus on three linked problems: the worldwide economic downturn, energy and security, and climate change. Annan said leaders needed to develop strong and effective policies, even bold or unconventional ones, to support lasting economic growth and generate employment for people who have lost their jobs.

Rupert Murdoch, chief executive of News Corp., said attendees had to be completely frank about the world’s current condition. He cautioned that the loss of $50 trillion in personal wealth had left many people discouraged and shaken. Murdoch said the Western world had been spending beyond its means, describing it as a long excess that had now ended and required a painful adjustment.

At the same time, Murdoch argued that the economic slump could provide an opening to confront problems such as energy supply and pollution. He said that whether the crisis continued for one year or five, it should be used as a chance to decide what goals should shape the recovery and to create policies that help address those broader challenges.

HSBC Chairman Stephen Green said the banking sector needed to acknowledge that it had performed poorly in the events leading to the financial collapse. He also urged governments to continue intervening in order to prevent a severe recession from worsening into something more dangerous. However, Green added that major banks also had a role to play in resolving the crisis, saying a strong economy cannot exist without effective and well-functioning international capital markets.

Werner Wenning said he did not expect this year’s forum to produce concrete answers, but hoped the participants could reach a shared understanding of what caused the financial crisis. He also called for a renewed commitment to the fundamentals of sustainable conduct. Wenning said that if the world can genuinely confront the major challenges ahead, trust in leadership can be rebuilt, adding that global leadership is urgently needed.

Political figures were expected to enter the debate later Wednesday, with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both scheduled to give major speeches setting out their priorities.

Kofi Annan told the World Economic Forum that the global recession had exposed not only weaknesses in the world economy, but also a deeper crisis in global governance. Speaking to political, business, and civil-society leaders, the former United Nations secretary-general said the financial turmoil had made clear that international institutions were struggling to respond effectively to problems that no country could solve alone.

Annan argued that the world had changed dramatically since many of today’s global institutions were created, yet the structures of power had not kept pace. He said the United Nations, in particular, needed far-reaching reform if it was to remain legitimate and effective in addressing modern challenges. Without such reform, he warned, global decision-making would continue to be hampered by outdated arrangements and a lack of trust among nations.

He pointed to the U.N. Security Council as one of the clearest examples of the problem. Its composition, shaped by the balance of power after the Second World War, no longer reflects the political and economic realities of the twenty-first century, he said. Emerging powers and regions that now play major roles in the global economy and international affairs must have a stronger voice in the institutions that make decisions on peace, security, and development.

Annan also emphasized that the recession had shown how closely connected the world’s major challenges had become. Economic recovery, energy security, climate change, poverty, and political stability could not be treated as separate issues, he said. Efforts to restore growth would not succeed in the long term unless they were linked to sustainable development and a more cooperative approach to managing shared risks.

He urged governments to move beyond narrow national interests and work together more seriously on common solutions. In his view, the world needed stronger multilateral cooperation, not less, at a time when economic uncertainty and environmental pressures were increasing. Protectionism, political rivalry, and short-term thinking, he suggested, would only deepen instability and make future crises more difficult to manage.

Annan warned that sustainable growth depended on a fairer and more inclusive global order. Countries that were becoming more influential economically and politically had to be brought into decision-making, while established powers had to accept that the old system could not simply continue unchanged. Reform, he said, was not only a matter of fairness but also a practical necessity for maintaining international stability.

His message to the forum was that the recession should be treated as a wake-up call. The crisis had revealed the limits of existing institutions and the dangers of fragmented responses to global problems. Only through renewed cooperation, broader representation, and serious reform of international bodies could the world build a more stable, secure, and sustainable future.

**Annan: Recession exposes “crisis of global governance,” demands U.N. reform**

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan warned world leaders gathered at the World Economic Forum that the global recession has exposed a deeper failure in the way international institutions manage shared crises, calling for sweeping reforms to make the United Nations and other global bodies more effective.

Speaking in Davos, Annan said the economic downturn was not simply a financial collapse, but a sign that global decision-making has failed to keep pace with an interconnected world.

“This is a crisis of global governance,” Annan told political and business leaders, arguing that institutions created in the aftermath of World War II are no longer equipped to respond quickly or fairly to modern challenges such as financial instability, climate change, poverty and conflict.

Annan called for “radical reform” of the United Nations, including changes to the Security Council, whose permanent membership still reflects the power structure of 1945 rather than today’s geopolitical realities. He said emerging powers and developing nations need a stronger voice in global decision-making if international institutions are to regain legitimacy.

The former U.N. chief said the recession had demonstrated how decisions made in one part of the world can rapidly affect millions elsewhere, particularly in poorer countries that had little role in creating the crisis but face severe consequences from shrinking trade, falling investment and rising unemployment.

Annan urged leaders at the forum to resist protectionism and short-term political fixes, warning that a fragmented response could deepen the downturn and increase instability. He said governments must cooperate on financial regulation, development, food security and climate policy.

The remarks came as the annual gathering in Davos was dominated by concern over the global financial crisis, with bankers, executives and heads of state facing sharp criticism over failures in oversight and accountability.

Annan said rebuilding confidence would require more than stimulus packages and rescue plans. It would require institutions that are transparent, representative and capable of acting decisively across borders.

“The world has changed,” he said. “Our institutions must change with it.”

**World Economic Forum opens in Davos with recession, governance and climate at center stage**

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — The World Economic Forum opened in the Swiss Alps with global business and political leaders confronting a stark agenda dominated by recession, financial instability, energy insecurity and climate change.

The first day of meetings in Davos reflected the scale of anxiety across markets and governments, as executives, policymakers and international figures debated whether the global downturn would produce deeper protectionism and geopolitical tension—or become a catalyst for reforming the institutions that manage the world economy.

Former United Nations Secretary-General **Kofi Annan** warned that the economic crisis had exposed serious weaknesses in global governance. He said the recession could not be addressed by governments acting alone and argued that international institutions needed to become more representative, effective and accountable.

Annan linked the financial crisis to broader challenges including poverty, security, food supply and climate change, saying that short-term economic rescue efforts should not push long-term development and environmental commitments off the agenda. He stressed that the poorest countries, though least responsible for the financial turmoil, were likely to suffer heavily from shrinking trade, falling investment and reduced aid flows.

Media executive **Rupert Murdoch** said the downturn had shaken confidence in business and finance, but he also argued that open markets and innovation remained essential to recovery. Murdoch cautioned against protectionism, saying that closing economies would make the recession worse and delay the return of growth. He also pointed to the role of information, communications and media in shaping public understanding of the crisis and holding leaders to account.

**Stephen Green**, chairman of **HSBC**, said the financial sector faced a long process of rebuilding trust after the banking crisis. He said banks, regulators and governments all had lessons to learn, including the need for stronger oversight, better risk management and more responsible lending practices. Green emphasized that the recession had become global in nature and said recovery would require cooperation between major economies, especially in restoring confidence to credit markets.

Green also noted that financial stability could not be separated from wider questions of social responsibility. He said the crisis had raised fundamental concerns about values in business and the purpose of financial institutions, adding that banks must demonstrate that they serve the real economy rather than operate only for short-term gain.

**Werner Wenning**, chief executive of **Bayer**, focused on the links between industry, energy security and climate change. He said companies were facing severe pressure from the recession, but warned that governments and businesses should not abandon investment in cleaner technologies, energy efficiency and innovation. Wenning argued that climate policy and industrial competitiveness should be pursued together, rather than treated as opposing goals.

Wenning said energy security remained a strategic concern for both developed and emerging economies, particularly as volatile energy prices and dependence on imports continued to affect business planning. He called for policies that encourage long-term investment in research, infrastructure and sustainable production.

Security concerns also featured prominently on the opening day. Participants discussed how the economic crisis could aggravate political instability, unemployment and social unrest in vulnerable regions. Annan and other speakers underlined that economic hardship, weak governance and insecurity often reinforce one another, making coordinated international action more urgent.

Climate change was another recurring theme, despite fears that the recession might push environmental issues down the priority list. Speakers argued that any recovery strategy should include investment in low-carbon infrastructure and energy efficiency, both to reduce emissions and to create new sources of growth.

The atmosphere in Davos was more sober than in previous years, with many participants acknowledging that the crisis had damaged faith in financial institutions and in the ability of governments to anticipate systemic risks. Still, the opening discussions also carried a message that the downturn could provide an opportunity to reshape global economic rules.

The central question emerging from the first day was whether world leaders could move beyond emergency responses and agree on a broader framework for recovery—one that addresses financial regulation, global governance, energy security, development and climate change together.

As the forum continued, delegates were expected to focus on practical steps to revive growth, reform financial markets and restore confidence in globalization at a moment when the global economy faced one of its most severe tests in decades.

**DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan. 24 —** Former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan warned that the United Nations Security Council risks losing legitimacy unless it is reshaped to reflect the shifting balance of global power, saying emerging economies must be given a stronger voice in decisions on international peace and security.

Speaking on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Annan said the Council’s structure still mirrors the geopolitical realities of the post-World War Two era, when the five permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France — were granted veto power.

That arrangement, he argued, no longer adequately represents a world in which countries such as India, Brazil, South Africa and other rising regional powers play increasingly important diplomatic, economic and military roles.

Annan said the credibility of the United Nations depends in part on whether its most powerful body is seen as broadly representative. Without reform, he suggested, decisions taken by the Council may face growing resistance from states that feel excluded from the process.

Diplomats and analysts have long debated proposals to expand the Council, including adding new permanent or long-term seats for major developing nations and under-represented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. But successive reform efforts have stalled amid disagreements over which countries should gain seats, whether new members should have veto rights, and how to balance regional rivalries.

Annan said the issue was not simply one of prestige for emerging powers, but of effectiveness. Global crises — from armed conflicts to terrorism, climate-related insecurity and humanitarian emergencies — increasingly require cooperation from a wider set of influential states, he said.

The former secretary-general has repeatedly called for multilateral institutions to adapt to changing realities, arguing that bodies created in the mid-20th century must evolve if they are to command confidence in the 21st.

Security Council reform remains one of the most politically sensitive issues at the United Nations. Any change to the Council’s composition would require approval by two-thirds of the U.N. General Assembly and ratification by the permanent members, each of which has the power to block amendments to the U.N. Charter.

**World Economic Forum opens with stark warnings over global crisis**

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — The World Economic Forum opened Wednesday in the Swiss Alpine resort of Davos with an unusually sober tone, as political leaders, central bankers and corporate executives gathered amid the worst global financial crisis in decades.

Kofi Annan, the former U.N. secretary-general and one of the meeting’s co-chairs, warned that the turmoil had exposed deep failures in the international system and said the world could not return to “business as usual.”

“Our global institutions are broken,” Annan told participants, arguing that the economic crisis had shown how closely connected markets had become — and how poorly equipped governments and multilateral bodies were to manage shocks that move rapidly across borders.

The annual gathering, long associated with confidence in globalization and free markets, is taking place this year under very different circumstances. Banks have collapsed or been rescued by governments, credit markets remain strained, unemployment is rising in many major economies, and fears of a prolonged global recession dominate the agenda.

The 2009 meeting’s theme, **“Shaping the Post-Crisis World,”** reflects a broad recognition among delegates that the financial meltdown has turned into a test of political leadership, regulatory oversight and public trust.

Business leaders arriving in Davos said the crisis had forced a fundamental reassessment of risk, debt and corporate responsibility. Many executives acknowledged that the banking system had been damaged not only by bad assets and excessive leverage, but also by a collapse of confidence among investors, consumers and institutions.

Several participants said restoring trust would require more transparency, tougher regulation and closer coordination among governments. Others cautioned that poorly designed regulation could deepen the downturn by discouraging lending or investment.

The atmosphere in Davos contrasted sharply with previous years, when discussion often focused on emerging markets, innovation, trade and the expansion of global finance. This year, the central questions are more urgent: how to stabilize banks, prevent further job losses, revive lending and avoid protectionism.

The crisis began in the U.S. housing and mortgage markets but quickly spread through the global financial system, bringing down major financial firms and forcing governments to commit trillions of dollars in support for banks and credit markets. By early 2009, the effects were being felt far beyond Wall Street, with factories cutting production, exports falling and households reducing spending.

World leaders and economists in Davos are expected to debate the appropriate scale of stimulus spending, the future of financial regulation and the role of institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and United Nations in responding to crises that cross national boundaries.

Annan’s warning echoed a broader theme among attendees: that the crisis is not simply a market failure, but a governance failure. The former U.N. chief said the world’s institutions must be rebuilt to reflect modern realities, including the growing influence of emerging economies and the need for coordinated responses to global problems.

The meeting also comes as the new U.S. administration of President Barack Obama begins work on additional measures to rescue the American economy. Although Obama is not attending the forum, his administration’s policies are expected to be closely watched by financial leaders and foreign officials.

European leaders, meanwhile, face pressure to balance stimulus efforts with concerns over rising public debt. Developing nations are warning that they risk being hit hardest by a crisis they did not create, as investment flows slow and demand for exports weakens.

In private sessions and public panels, corporate executives are expected to discuss executive compensation, banking reform, corporate governance and the responsibility of business in rebuilding confidence. Many leaders in Davos say the credibility of both markets and elites has been badly damaged.

Despite the bleak mood, organizers and participants said the forum provides a rare opportunity for leaders from government, business and civil society to speak directly at a moment of global uncertainty.

The question hanging over Davos is whether the discussions will lead to meaningful action — or whether the crisis will continue to outpace the ability of governments and institutions to respond.

**Davos opens under recession cloud with calls for reform, restraint and trust**

DAVOS, Switzerland — The World Economic Forum opened against the stark backdrop of a deepening global recession, with business and political leaders using their first remarks to acknowledge a crisis not only of markets, but of confidence in the institutions that had guided globalization.

Former U.N. Secretary-General **Kofi Annan** said the downturn had exposed weaknesses in international governance and renewed the need to make global institutions more representative and effective. Speaking about U.N. reform, Annan warned that change could not be cosmetic: **“The U.N. is a mirror of its member states,”** he said, arguing that meaningful reform would depend on governments’ willingness to modernize the system and share responsibility for global problems.

Media executive **Rupert Murdoch** struck a blunt tone on the causes of the financial crisis, describing the years preceding the crash as an era of excess. The world economy, he said, had gone through an unsustainable **“binge”** of borrowing, speculation and easy credit, leaving governments, companies and consumers to deal with the consequences. His remarks reflected a broader mood in Davos: that recovery would require not simply stimulus, but a reassessment of the habits that fueled the boom.

From the banking sector, **Stephen Green**, chairman of HSBC, acknowledged the damage done to public confidence by financial institutions. Banks, he said, had to accept responsibility for restoring discipline and credibility. Green emphasized that the industry needed to return to its core purpose of serving the real economy rather than chasing excessive risk, saying in effect that banks must rebuild trust by becoming more transparent, better governed and more prudent.

**Werner Wenning**, chief executive of Bayer, said the recession had produced a wider crisis of leadership. Restoring confidence, he argued, would require executives and policymakers to demonstrate responsibility beyond short-term results. **“Trust in leadership has to be restored,”** Wenning said, stressing that leaders must show integrity, accountability and a commitment to long-term stability.

The opening exchanges set the tone for a Davos meeting defined less by celebration of globalization than by sober reflection on its failures. Participants repeatedly returned to the same themes: reform of international institutions, tighter oversight of finance, restraint after years of excess, and the need for leaders to rebuild public trust in a shaken global system.
